business_model: Subscription short-form mobile-only video, high original-content spend

historical_evidence.company: Founded by Jeffrey Katzenberg (former DreamWorks Animation CEO, former Disney studio chairman) with Meg Whitman (former HP/eBay CEO) as CEO, building a mobile-only short-form ('quick bites') premium streaming video service, still roughly six months from commercial launch at the snapshot date.
historical_evidence.market: The mobile short-form video attention market was already large and dominated by free, ad-supported/creator-driven platforms (TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat); Quibi's premium, subscription, studio-produced content model was a structurally different bet within an already-crowded attention category.
historical_evidence.team: Katzenberg and Whitman are both proven, exceptionally credentialed executives with major prior successes (DreamWorks Animation, HP/eBay respectively), though neither had a specific prior track record building a mobile-video or short-form-content consumer product.
historical_evidence.product: Built around proprietary 'Turnstyle' technology enabling seamless switching between portrait and landscape viewing, with content produced specifically and only for mobile-phone consumption — a genuinely novel technical/format bet, paired with a large committed content budget (publicly reported plans to spend up to $1B on programming through 2025).
historical_evidence.execution: Raised $1 billion pre-launch from a roster of major film studios (Disney, WarnerMedia, NBCUniversal, Sony, and others) on the strength of its executive team's reputations — an unusually large pre-launch, pre-product-market-fit capital commitment.
historical_evidence.traction: None — the product had not yet launched commercially as of the snapshot date, so no user, subscriber, or engagement data exists to evaluate; this is expected and correct for a pre-launch company, not an evidence gap.
historical_evidence.financial: Contemporaneous coverage (as of the snapshot date) explicitly noted that industry insiders privately expressed skepticism about whether mobile-obsessed, younger consumers would pay for a glossier, studio-produced alternative to free platforms like TikTok — a real, contemporaneously-reported note of caution existing alongside the massive capital commitment, not a retrospective judgment invented after the product's later failure. ENRICHED (see benchmark_notes): the same Digiday pitch-deck reporting already cited in this record discloses more specific committed-spend figures than originally extracted — a 'base case' investor plan of 20 million subscribers within five years, first-year content spend of $600M scaling to as much as $978M by year five, and per-minute content costs of $10,000-$125,000 (comparable to or exceeding broadcast-TV per-minute costs) for short-form content. This is real, dated, Financial-Health/Burn-Efficiency-relevant evidence of the capital intensity and revenue assumptions underlying the business plan, not merely the aggregate raise figure.

normalized_facts.note: added during dimension-coverage search — extracted from an already-cited source, not a new one; this is an investor-pitch target, not an achieved figure
